Find and fix what's broken in an Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) Automatic cluster, one challenge at a time. In this capture-the-flag lab, each challenge is a realistic fault, already in place in its own namespace of your cluster. You investigate with the tools on your lab VM, restore the expected behavior, and check your work with one command. Every challenge that passes its check is a captured flag.

**Level:** 200, intermediate  
**Duration:** about 3 hours, in rounds of 15 to 30 minutes

## How the lab works

1. A proctor introduces a challenge, what success looks like, and the tools that can help.
1. You investigate on your own, with the evidence in your environment, and restore the expected outcome. Each challenge page has hints that you can expand, and proctors can give more.
1. You check your work with one command. A challenge that passes is a captured flag.
1. At the end of the round, a proctor shows one way to fix the challenge, and explains the troubleshooting path.
1. The room moves on to the next challenge. Challenges are independent, so you can start the next one even if you didn't finish the last one.

## Your lab environment

Everything in the following table is ready for you. You don't need your own Azure subscription or local tools.

| Component | What's ready for you |
|:--|:--|
| Lab VM | Visual Studio Code with GitHub Copilot and the AKS-MCP server, AKS desktop, the Azure CLI, `kubectl`, `kubelogin`, Helm, `ingress2gateway`, the GitHub CLI, PowerShell 7, Git Bash, and WSL with Ubuntu |
| AKS Automatic cluster | **aks-kubecon-ctf**, in resource group **@lab.CloudResourceGroup(ResourceGroup1).Name**, with node autoprovisioning, deployment safeguards, Azure RBAC, workload identity, the application routing add-on with Gateway API, and Managed Prometheus |
| Challenges | Each in its own namespace of your cluster, each with its fault already in place |
| **C:\lab-resources** | The challenge instructions, and the scripts that check your work and start a challenge over |

## The challenges

| ID | Challenge | Namespace | Suggested time |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| C1 | The store won't start | `c1-store` | 15–20 minutes |
| C2 | Move the storefront to Gateway API | `c2-storefront` | 25–30 minutes |
| C3 | Capacity that never arrives | `c3-processing` (plus the cluster-scoped NodePool `c3-processing`) | 20–25 minutes |
| C4 | The AI assistant is up, but not working | `c4-assistant` | 20–25 minutes |
| A1 | Where did DNS go? | `a1-inventory` | 20–25 minutes |
| A2 | Fast yesterday, slow today | `a2-checkout` | 20–25 minutes |
| A3 | Ready for maintenance? | `a3-maintenance` | 20–25 minutes |
| A4 | Identity without secrets | `a4-config` | 20–25 minutes |
| A5 | Running is not ready | `a5-releases` | 15–20 minutes |
| A6 | The data survived, the application didn't | `a6-records` | 20–25 minutes |

Your proctor tells you which challenge each round uses. C1 to C4 are the core challenges, and A1 to A6 are alternates. Finished a round early? Try an alternate.

## How to use these instructions

- Commands appear as type text. Select the terminal in the lab VM first, and then select a command in these instructions to type it there. Press **Enter** to run it.
- Code blocks show commands to copy or adapt. They're written for bash, and most `kubectl` commands work unchanged in PowerShell. **Tools and tips** describes how to run the bash-only ones.
- Select the checkbox next to each step when you finish it.

> [!Note] You need basic familiarity with containers and Kubernetes: pods, deployments, services, and `kubectl`. Each challenge page describes what's running, what success looks like, and how to check your work.

## Tips for AKS Automatic

AKS Automatic enforces [deployment safeguards](https://aka.ms/aks/deployment-safeguards) and a baseline pod security
policy, which changes a few familiar debugging habits:

* **Prefer `kubectl exec` into the application's own pods** – every challenge image includes the tools you need (`curl`/`wget`, `getent`/`nslookup`).
* A throw-away `kubectl run` pod is **denied** unless it sets resource requests:
  `kubectl run dbg -n <ns> --image=mcr.microsoft.com/azurelinux/busybox:1.36 --restart=Never --overrides='{"apiVersion":"v1","spec":{"containers":[{"name":"dbg","image":"mcr.microsoft.com/azurelinux/busybox:1.36","command":["sleep","600"],"resources":{"requests":{"cpu":"100m","memory":"128Mi"}}}]}}'`
  (missing probes only produce warnings).
* `kubectl debug` works with the **baseline** or **restricted** profile:
  `kubectl debug -n <ns> <pod> -it --image=mcr.microsoft.com/azurelinux/busybox:1.36 --profile=baseline -- sh`.
  The default/`general` profile adds `SYS_PTRACE` and is rejected.
* `kubectl apply` prints `Warning: <name> had anti-affinity and topology spread constraints added ...` for most
  Deployments – that is the safeguards mutating policy, not an error.
* Pods resolve DNS through **LocalDNS**, a cache on every node (`nameserver 169.254.10.11` in `/etc/resolv.conf`).
* An occasional `Error from server (InternalError)` that mentions `guard` or `subjectaccessreviews` is the cluster's
  Azure RBAC authorization check timing out: run the command again.

# Check your work, or start over

## Check your work

Each challenge page ends its success criteria with a check command, such as:

+++C:\lab-resources\check.ps1 c1+++

The check runs the challenge's success criteria against your cluster, and shows **PASS** or **FAIL** for each one, then **PASSED** or **NOT PASSED** for the challenge. **PASSED** is a captured flag. A check takes a minute or two, because some checks watch the application for 60 seconds. C3 can wait several minutes for a new node.

- For a quicker, less strict look while you work, add `-Quick`.
- To check several challenges, separate them with commas, such as `c1,a2`. With no challenge, it checks every challenge in your cluster.

> [!Note] If your event has a leaderboard, each check records your result there, with your first name and last initial. To keep a run off the leaderboard, add `-NoReport`. Runs with `-Quick` are never recorded.

## Start a challenge over

To start a challenge over, run its reset command, such as:

+++C:\lab-resources\reset.ps1 c1+++

The reset asks you to confirm, deletes the challenge's namespace, and deploys the challenge again with its fault. Your changes to that challenge are lost, and other challenges aren't touched. A reset takes 2 to 5 minutes. Some resets also reset Azure resources:

| Challenge | The reset also |
|:--|:--|
| C2 | Deletes your gateway and its public IP address |
| C3 | Deletes the challenge's node pool and its nodes |
| A4 | Resets the federated identity credential in Azure |
| A6 | Re-creates the disk and its data |

> [!Alert] Reset only the challenge that you're working on. A reset can't be undone.

# C1 · The store won't start

| | |
|---|---|
| **Namespace** | `c1-store` |
| **Suggested time** | 15–20 minutes |
| **Azure services** | AKS Automatic only |

## Participant briefing

> A configuration rollout has taken the order service offline. Restore order
> processing **without reverting the entire application**.

## Learning objective

Use events, previous-container logs and configuration to diagnose and repair an
application startup failure.

## What's running

The AKS Store demo (v2.2.0): `store-front` (web UI) → `order-service` (Node.js /
Fastify) → `rabbitmq` (order queue), plus `product-service`. `order-service` reads
its settings from the ConfigMap `order-service-configs` and the Secret
`order-service-secrets`.

```bash
kubectl get all -n c1-store
# Open the store UI (optional):
kubectl port-forward -n c1-store svc/store-front 8080:80   # http://localhost:8080
```

## Success criteria

1. `order-service` has all required replicas **Ready**.
2. Restart counts do **not** increase during a 60-second observation after the rollout.
3. A synthetic order (`POST /api/orders` through the storefront) succeeds and lands in the `orders` queue.
4. The fix lives in the **authoritative configuration** (the ConfigMap), not in a temporary override that
   disappears on the next deployment.

Check your work:

+++C:\lab-resources\check.ps1 c1+++

## Hints

> [+Hint] Hint 1 – Find the component that is failing to become ready
>
> `kubectl get pods -n c1-store` – which pod is not `Running`/`Ready`, and what does `kubectl describe pod`
> say in its **Events**?

> [+Hint] Hint 2 – Inspect logs from the previous container instance
>
> A crash-looping container has already exited; its logs are on the *previous* instance:
> `kubectl logs -n c1-store deploy/order-service --previous`. Read the whole log – the real error is
> above some unrelated `npm notice` lines.

> [+Hint] Hint 3 – Trace the rejected setting to its configuration source
>
> Where does the container get its environment from? (`kubectl describe deployment order-service -n c1-store`,
> look for `Environment Variables from`). Environment variables are read when a container **starts** – what
> has to happen after you change the source?

## What doesn't count

* `kubectl set env` / editing the Deployment to override the value (a temporary edit the next deployment
  would undo).
* Rolling back the whole application or deleting the ConfigMap.

## Stretch objective

Explain why restarting the pod alone did not fix the issue, and propose a pre-deployment configuration check
that would have caught it.

## Reset

To start this challenge over, run the following command, and confirm. Your changes to this challenge are lost.

+++C:\lab-resources\reset.ps1 c1+++

The reset re-creates the challenge with its fault.

# C2 · Move the storefront to Gateway API

| | |
|---|---|
| **Namespace** | `c2-storefront` |
| **Suggested time** | 25–30 minutes |
| **Azure services** | AKS Automatic with the **application routing add-on**: managed NGINX (IngressClass `webapprouting.kubernetes.azure.com`) and the add-on's Istio-based **Gateway API** implementation (GatewayClass `approuting-istio`); Azure Load Balancer public IPs with an Azure-provided DNS name |
| **Tools** | `kubectl`, `curl`, [`ingress2gateway`](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/ingress2gateway) (the Kubernetes SIG Network migration tool), an AI assistant of your choice |

## Participant briefing

> The storefront is published through **Ingress-NGINX** – the managed NGINX of the AKS application routing
> add-on. The upstream Ingress-NGINX project is retired, and Microsoft-supported security patches for the
> add-on's NGINX end in **November 2026**. Platform engineering has already enabled the add-on's **Gateway API**
> implementation on this cluster.
>
> Move the storefront to Gateway API **without a big-bang outage**: translate the existing Ingress with
> `ingress2gateway`, have an AI assistant adapt the draft for AKS (and check its work), validate the new path
> side by side with the old one, then cut the public name over to the gateway and decommission the Ingress.
>
> The storefront's public name, `ctf-store-<id>.<region>.cloudapp.azure.com`, is reserved for the go-live: it
> starts resolving when you publish it on the gateway.

## Learning objective

Run an Ingress → Gateway API migration on AKS end to end: inventory, automated translation, AI-assisted (and
human-verified) adaptation, side-by-side validation, DNS cutover and decommissioning.

## What's running

* AKS Store demo: `store-front`, `product-service`, `order-service`, `rabbitmq` (all `ClusterIP` Services).
* Ingress `storefront` (class `webapprouting.kubernetes.azure.com`) for the storefront's host name, served by the
  add-on's shared NGINX controller (Service `nginx` in `app-routing-system`: one public IP for every Ingress).
* GatewayClass `approuting-istio` – ready to use; no Gateway exists yet.

```bash
kubectl get ingress,svc,pods -n c2-storefront
kubectl get ingressclass,gatewayclass
STORE_HOST=$(kubectl get ingress storefront -n c2-storefront -o jsonpath='{.spec.rules[0].host}')
INGRESS_IP=$(kubectl get ingress storefront -n c2-storefront -o jsonpath='{.status.loadBalancer.ingress[0].ip}')
curl -s --resolve "$STORE_HOST:80:$INGRESS_IP" "http://$STORE_HOST/" | grep -o '<title>.*</title>'   # today: via NGINX
```

```powershell
$STORE_HOST = kubectl get ingress storefront -n c2-storefront -o jsonpath='{.spec.rules[0].host}'
$INGRESS_IP = kubectl get ingress storefront -n c2-storefront -o jsonpath='{.status.loadBalancer.ingress[0].ip}'
curl.exe -s --resolve "${STORE_HOST}:80:${INGRESS_IP}" "http://$STORE_HOST/" | Select-String '<title>'
```

`--resolve` sends a request for the real host name to an IP you choose – the usual way to test a front door
before DNS points at it. **Don't browse to the name before the cutover**: a "name does not exist" answer can be
cached for up to 5 minutes.

### How public names work here

Azure creates `<label>.<region>.cloudapp.azure.com` for a load balancer's public IP when the Kubernetes Service
behind it has the annotation `service.beta.kubernetes.io/azure-dns-label-name: <label>`. A Gateway passes
annotations to the Service it generates through `spec.infrastructure.annotations`. The storefront's label:

```bash
kubectl get namespace c2-storefront -o jsonpath='{.metadata.annotations.kubecon\.lab/storefront-dns-label}{"\n"}'
```

### Your tools

**ingress2gateway** translates Ingress resources (and ingress-nginx annotations) into Gateway API resources. It
reads from your current kubectl context or from a file and prints the result – it never changes the cluster.

Your lab VM already has `ingress2gateway`. To check, run:

+++ingress2gateway version+++

**An AI assistant** – GitHub Copilot (Chat in VS Code or the Copilot CLI; the Free plan is enough), Copilot in
Azure (the Copilot button in the Azure portal), or any assistant you use. A starting prompt:

> I'm migrating an app on AKS from the application routing add-on's managed NGINX (Ingress) to Gateway API with
> the add-on's Istio-based implementation, GatewayClass `approuting-istio`. Below are the existing Ingress and
> the draft ingress2gateway produced, including its warnings. Adapt the draft so it works on this cluster. Keep
> the host name, path and backend unchanged and don't add TLS. Explain every change and anything I should
> double-check before applying it.
>
> *(paste the Ingress YAML, the ingress2gateway output and its warnings)*

**AI drafts, you verify.** Before you apply anything, check the GatewayClass, the Gateway's name (it becomes
part of the generated Deployment and Service names), that the HTTPRoute's `parentRefs` point at your Gateway, that
host name, path, backend Service and port match the Ingress, and the request timeout ingress2gateway derived from
the `proxy-read-timeout` annotation.

## Success criteria

1. A Gateway of class `approuting-istio` in `c2-storefront` is **programmed** with a public IP, and an HTTPRoute
   attached to it serves the storefront's host name (`PathPrefix /` → Service `store-front` port 80) – route
   status **Accepted**, references **resolved**.
2. **Cutover:** `http://<storefront host name>/` resolves to the gateway and returns the storefront (HTTP 200,
   "Contoso Pet Store"); other host names get 404 from the gateway.
3. **Decommissioned:** no Ingress is left in `c2-storefront`; `store-front` is still `ClusterIP` and the gateway is
   the namespace's only public endpoint.

Check your work:

+++C:\lab-resources\check.ps1 c2+++

## Hints

> [+Hint] Hint 1 – ingress2gateway says "No resources found"
>
> Its ingress-nginx provider only reads Ingresses of class `nginx` unless you tell it otherwise. Which class does
> the storefront's Ingress use? Look at `ingress2gateway print --help` for an ingress-class flag, and use
> `--providers=ingress-nginx --namespace c2-storefront`. (Offline alternative:
> `kubectl get ingress storefront -n c2-storefront -o yaml > ingress.yaml` and `--input-file ingress.yaml`.)

> [+Hint] Hint 2 – The Gateway never becomes programmed
>
> `kubectl get gateway -n c2-storefront` – look at `CLASS` and `PROGRAMMED`. The draft reuses the IngressClass
> name as the GatewayClass (`kubectl get gatewayclass`); on AKS the Gateway API implementation is
> `approuting-istio`. Give the Gateway a short name that is a valid DNS label, such as `store-gateway`: the
> gateway's Deployment and Service are called `<gateway-name>-approuting-istio`. Point the HTTPRoute's `parentRefs`
> at that name. `kubectl describe gateway <name> -n c2-storefront` shows why a Gateway isn't programmed.

> [+Hint] Hint 3 – Validate side by side, before any DNS change
>
> ```bash
> kubectl wait --for=condition=Programmed gateway/<name> -n c2-storefront --timeout=5m
> GW_IP=$(kubectl get gateway <name> -n c2-storefront -o jsonpath='{.status.addresses[0].value}')
> curl -s --resolve "$STORE_HOST:80:$GW_IP" "http://$STORE_HOST/" | grep -o '<title>.*</title>'      # the storefront
> curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' -H 'Host: not-the-store.example' "http://$GW_IP/"      # 404
> kubectl describe httproute -n c2-storefront                                    # Accepted / ResolvedRefs
> kubectl logs -n c2-storefront deploy/<name>-approuting-istio --tail=5          # the gateway's access log
> ```
>
> The old path through NGINX keeps working the whole time – nothing has changed for customers yet.

> [+Hint] Hint 4 – Cut over, then decommission
>
> Publish the name on the gateway (see *How public names work here*): add `spec.infrastructure.annotations` with
> `service.beta.kubernetes.io/azure-dns-label-name: <label>` to your Gateway and re-apply it. Within a minute or
> so `nslookup <storefront host name>` returns the gateway's IP. Open `http://<storefront host name>/` in a
> browser – then delete the Ingress.

## What doesn't count

* Exposing `store-front` as a `LoadBalancer`/`NodePort` Service, or port-forwarding.
* Leaving the Ingress in place – or deleting it before the gateway serves the storefront (big-bang).
* Publishing the storefront under a different host name.

## Stretch objectives

* Map the Ingress fields to Gateway API: which part of the `Ingress` became the `Gateway`, which the `HTTPRoute`?
  What did the `proxy-read-timeout` annotation turn into, and is that equivalent?
* Why does the gateway get its own load balancer IP while NGINX served every Ingress from one shared IP?
* Production follow-up: once no Ingress uses the add-on's NGINX, it is turned off with
  `az aks approuting update -g <resource-group> -n <cluster> --nginx None`. That is cluster-wide – **don't** do it
  in the lab.

## Troubleshooting

* **curl works but the browser doesn't** – type the full `http://` URL (browsers may try HTTPS first; the
  gateway only listens on port 80), use a private window (cached error pages or DNS answers), and check whether a
  VPN or corporate proxy blocks `*.cloudapp.azure.com`.
* **The name doesn't resolve after the cutover** – give it a minute. `kubectl get svc -n c2-storefront` should show
  the gateway's Service with your label annotation; `kubectl describe svc <name>-approuting-istio -n c2-storefront`
  shows load-balancer events (for example a label already in use). If you looked the name up before the cutover,
  your resolver may cache "does not exist" for up to 5 minutes: compare with `nslookup <host> 8.8.8.8`.

## Reset

To start this challenge over, run the following command, and confirm. Your changes to this challenge are lost.

+++C:\lab-resources\reset.ps1 c2+++

The reset re-creates the challenge with its fault.

# C3 · Capacity that never arrives

| | |
|---|---|
| **Namespace** | `c3-processing` (plus the cluster-scoped NodePool `c3-processing`) |
| **Suggested time** | 20–25 minutes, including 1–5 minutes of node provisioning after the fix |
| **Azure services** | AKS Automatic node auto-provisioning (NAP, Karpenter-based) |

## Participant briefing

> A new order-processing batch job is stuck `Pending`. Node auto-provisioning is enabled, but the capacity it
> needs never appears. Get the batch to run **on its dedicated processing pool**.
>
> Platform standards for the processing pool: general-purpose **D-family**, **2–4 vCPU**, on-demand, nodes
> reserved for processing workloads (label + taint). The processing image is published for **amd64 only**.

## Learning objective

Relate workload scheduling requirements to NodePool eligibility and explain why useful capacity is not
provisioned.

## What's running

* Job `order-batch` (namespace `c3-processing`) – requires `kubecon.lab/pool=processing`,
  `kubernetes.io/arch=amd64` and tolerates the processing taint.
* NAP `NodePool` `c3-processing` (cluster-scoped, `karpenter.sh/v1`) – the dedicated pool for that workload.
* AKS Automatic's own NodePools (`default`, `system-surge`) also exist.

```bash
kubectl get pods,jobs -n c3-processing
kubectl get nodepools
```

## Success criteria

1. The batch Job **completes** on capacity from the **dedicated** NodePool `c3-processing`.
2. The workload keeps its placement, architecture (`amd64`) and isolation requirements (no removing the
   nodeSelector/toleration, no moving it to unrelated capacity).
3. The NodePool keeps its isolation (label + `NoSchedule` taint), its CPU limit and its `amd64` requirement –
   you make its requirements *satisfiable*, you don't delete all constraints.

Check your work:

+++C:\lab-resources\check.ps1 c3+++

## Hints

> [+Hint] Hint 1 – Follow the Pending pod's scheduling evidence
>
> `kubectl describe pod -n c3-processing -l app=order-batch` – read **all** the Events, including those from
> the node auto-provisioner (Karpenter), not just the default scheduler's. Karpenter explains why the pools it
> *considered* don't fit – a pool that can't offer any instance type isn't mentioned at all, so don't take its
> "typo of ..." suggestion at face value.

> [+Hint] Hint 2 – Identify the pools eligible for this workload
>
> Which NodePool could ever host this pod (label + taint)? `kubectl get nodepools`, then
> `kubectl describe nodepool c3-processing` – its requirements **and its Events**. Note that a NodePool can
> report `READY=True` and still be unable to launch anything.

> [+Hint] Hint 3 – Look for constraints that cannot be satisfied together
>
> Compare every requirement in the NodePool with each other, not just with the pod. What does the `p` in
> an Azure VM size such as `Standard_D4ps_v6` mean? (`az vm list-skus -l <region> --size Standard_D4ps_v6 --query "[0].capabilities[?name=='CpuArchitectureType'].value"`)

## What doesn't count

* Removing the Job's `nodeSelector`/toleration, switching it to `arm64`, or running it on the `default` pool.
* Removing the NodePool's taint, label, CPU limit or architecture requirement, or deleting the NodePool.

## Stretch objective

Explain how these would look different in the evidence: an impossible selector combination, a pool resource
limit, Azure vCPU quota exhaustion, and temporary SKU unavailability in a zone.

## Reset

To start this challenge over, run the following command, and confirm. Your changes to this challenge are lost.

+++C:\lab-resources\reset.ps1 c3+++

The reset deletes the NodePool (and its nodes) and re-creates it.

Allow 2–5 minutes for the reset: deleting the NodePool drains and removes nodes from a previous successful
run, so retained nodes cannot mask the fault.

# C4 · The AI assistant is up, but not working

| | |
|---|---|
| **Namespace** | `c4-assistant` |
| **Suggested time** | 20–25 minutes |
| **Azure services** | Microsoft Foundry (Azure OpenAI) account with a `GlobalStandard` model deployment, a user-assigned managed identity with workload identity federation |

## Participant briefing

> The store's AI assistant passes all its health checks, but every time store staff click **Ask AI
> Assistant** to write a product description, it fails. Restore a successful end-to-end interaction.

## Learning objective

Trace an application request into an AI dependency and distinguish a configuration failure from Kubernetes
health.

## What's running

The AKS Store demo admin experience: `store-admin` (UI) → `product-service` → `ai-service` (Python/FastAPI,
OpenAI SDK) → a model deployment in a Microsoft Foundry (Azure OpenAI) account. `ai-service` authenticates
with **Microsoft Entra workload identity** (no API keys; key authentication is disabled on the account).
Supporting services: `order-service`, `makeline-service`, `rabbitmq`, `documentdb`.

```bash
kubectl get pods -n c4-assistant
kubectl port-forward -n c4-assistant svc/store-admin 8081:80     # http://localhost:8081
# Products -> edit (or add) a product -> "Ask AI Assistant"
```

## Success criteria

1. A synthetic request through the store (`store-admin` → `product-service` → `ai-service`) invokes the
   intended model deployment and returns a description (exact wording/quality does not matter).
2. The fix lives in the application's configuration; no credentials are hard-coded, access controls are not
   weakened, and there is no fabricated fallback response.

Check your work:

+++C:\lab-resources\check.ps1 c4+++

## Hints

> [+Hint] Hint 1 – Test useful functionality rather than pod status
>
> All pods are Ready because `/health` doesn't call the model. Trigger a real request (UI button, or
> `kubectl exec -n c4-assistant deploy/store-admin -- wget -q -O - --header 'Content-Type: application/json' --post-data '{"name":"Catnip Kicker","tags":["toy","cat"]}' http://localhost:8081/api/ai/generate/description`).

> [+Hint] Hint 2 – Inspect the failed dependency call
>
> `kubectl logs -n c4-assistant deploy/ai-service` – what did Azure OpenAI answer? Then check which endpoint and
> deployment the service is configured to call: `kubectl exec -n c4-assistant deploy/ai-service -- printenv | grep AZURE_OPENAI`.

> [+Hint] Hint 3 – Compare the configured deployment name with the actual deployments
>
> Where does `ai-service` get `AZURE_OPENAI_DEPLOYMENT_NAME`? Compare it with the deployments that exist in the
> Foundry account: `az cognitiveservices account deployment list -g <resource-group> -n <account> -o table`
> (or the Microsoft Foundry portal). Model upgrades usually come with a *new deployment* – check the change
> ticket on the ConfigMap.

## What doesn't count

* Switching `ai-service` to API keys (`USE_AZURE_AD=False`, adding `AZURE_OPENAI_API_KEY`), re-enabling key
  auth on the account, or granting broader Azure roles.
* Pointing `ai-service` at a bare model name such as `gpt-6-luna`: Foundry accounts answer those too, but that
  bypasses the provisioned deployment (its capacity, quota and policies) – use the deployment the platform team
  created.
* Re-creating a deployment with the old name, or returning a canned description.

## Stretch objective

Propose readiness, dependency telemetry and error handling that would make this failure easier to detect,
without making transient model errors restart the pod.

# A1 · Where did DNS go?

| | |
|---|---|
| **Namespace** | `a1-inventory` |
| **Suggested time** | 20–25 minutes |
| **Azure services** | AKS Automatic (Azure CNI powered by Cilium enforces NetworkPolicy; LocalDNS) |

## Participant briefing

> After a network-isolation change, `inventory-sync` can no longer reach the catalog API it depends on.
> Restore access **without opening unrestricted egress** – `inventory-sync` must still be unable to reach
> anything other than what it needs (for example the `ledger-api` or the internet).

## Learning objective

Separate DNS, connectivity and application failure; repair network policy without removing isolation.

## What's running

* `inventory-sync` – syncs the catalog every few seconds; logs every attempt and serves its last result at
  `/status`.
* `catalog-api` – the dependency `inventory-sync` is allowed to call.
* `ledger-api` – a sensitive service `inventory-sync` must **not** reach.
* NetworkPolicies from change CHG-1150.

```bash
kubectl get pods,svc,networkpolicy -n a1-inventory
kubectl logs -n a1-inventory deploy/inventory-sync --tail=5
```

The `inventory-sync` image includes `curl` and `getent` for testing from inside the pod:
`kubectl exec -n a1-inventory deploy/inventory-sync -- getent hosts catalog-api`.

## Success criteria

Tested **from inside `inventory-sync`** (so its policy applies):

1. Name resolution works and the application transaction (`GET http://catalog-api:8080/items`) succeeds.
2. A prohibited destination is still blocked (`ledger-api`, the internet).
3. Namespace isolation remains: `default-deny-egress` is unchanged and no policy allows unrestricted egress.
4. You did not edit cluster-wide DNS (CoreDNS / kube-system) or delete the policies.

Check your work:

+++C:\lab-resources\check.ps1 a1+++

## Hints

> [+Hint] Hint 1 – Test name resolution independently
>
> Does the name resolve? Does the service answer if you skip DNS?
> `kubectl exec ... -- getent hosts catalog-api` vs.
> `kubectl exec ... -- curl -s -m 3 http://$(kubectl get svc catalog-api -n a1-inventory -o jsonpath='{.spec.clusterIP}'):8080/items`.

> [+Hint] Hint 2 – Inspect the workload's effective egress policy
>
> Which policies select the `inventory-sync` pod? `kubectl get networkpolicy -n a1-inventory -o yaml` – egress
> from a pod is allowed only if *some* policy selecting it allows that destination and port.

> [+Hint] Hint 3 – Compare DNS traffic and destinations with the allow rules
>
> Where does the pod actually send DNS queries? `kubectl exec ... -- cat /etc/resolv.conf`. DNS uses port 53 over
> **UDP and TCP**. On AKS Automatic the answer is **LocalDNS**, a DNS cache on every node (`169.254.10.11`) – not
> the CoreDNS pods.

> [+Hint] Hint 4 – When the "textbook" DNS rule doesn't work
>
> With Azure CNI powered by Cilium, traffic to the node-local LocalDNS listener counts as traffic to the node
> itself (the Cilium `host` entity). A Kubernetes NetworkPolicy can't select the node: rules that allow 53 to the
> `k8s-app=kube-dns` pods or to `ipBlock` `169.254.10.x` don't match. Either allow port 53 without restricting the
> destination, or use a `CiliumNetworkPolicy` with `toEntities: [host]`
> ([AKS docs](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/aks/azure-cni-powered-by-cilium#is-aks-local-dns-supported-with-azure-cni-powered-by-cilium)).

## What doesn't count

* Deleting `default-deny-egress` or `inventory-sync-egress`, or adding an "allow all egress" rule.
* Allowing all UDP (or all ports) to everywhere, editing CoreDNS, or changing the app to use IP addresses.

## Stretch objective

Explain why opening all UDP traffic or deleting the policy fixes the symptom but fails the security requirement.
(Optional: trace DNS with Inspektor Gadget, e.g. `kubectl gadget run trace_dns -n a1-inventory`, if it is
available in your environment.)

+++C:\lab-resources\reset.ps1 a1+++

The reset re-creates the challenge with its fault.

# A2 · Fast yesterday, slow today

| | |
|---|---|
| **Namespace** | `a2-checkout` |
| **Suggested time** | 20–25 minutes |
| **Azure services** | AKS Automatic with **Azure Monitor managed service for Prometheus** – viewed through **Dashboards with Grafana** in the Azure portal (no Grafana instance to run); metrics-server for `kubectl top` |

## Participant briefing

> A resource-policy change ("right-size checkout-api", CHG-1163) has made checkout slow. Customers notice;
> `kubectl top` says the service is barely busy. Find out what the platform's metrics say, then restore the
> response-time objective **without giving the service unlimited resources**.
>
> Objective (fixed load test: 120 checkouts, concurrency 4): **p95 ≤ 300 ms, 0 errors**.
> Approved envelope for `checkout-api`: CPU limit ≤ 1 CPU per container, memory ≤ 512Mi, at most 2 replicas,
> limits must stay set. (Also in the ConfigMap `checkout-slo`.)

## Learning objective

Use the cluster's **Managed Prometheus** metrics (the AKS Automatic default) to correlate latency, CPU usage,
CPU **throttling** and resource configuration – then tune within an approved resource budget.

## What's running

* `checkout-api` – CPU-bound (every checkout verifies an order token with PBKDF2). `GET /stats` reports the
  container's cgroup CPU quota and throttling counters.
* `loadgen` – sends steady background "customer" traffic (about one checkout per second) and runs the fixed,
  bounded load test on demand. Its log shows what customers experience (p50/p95 every 30 s).
* The cluster sends its metrics to an Azure Monitor workspace (Managed Prometheus), so the
  **Kubernetes / Compute Resources** dashboards in the Azure portal show this namespace without any setup.

```bash
kubectl get pods,deploy,limitrange -n a2-checkout
kubectl get configmap checkout-slo -n a2-checkout -o jsonpath='{.data.README\.txt}'
kubectl logs -n a2-checkout deploy/loadgen --tail=3                         # what customers see right now
kubectl exec -n a2-checkout deploy/loadgen -- python3 /app/loadtest.py      # ~40-60 s while slow
```

**Dashboards:** Azure portal → your AKS cluster → **Monitoring** → **Dashboards with Grafana** →
**Kubernetes / Compute Resources / Pod** (type *Compute Resources* in the search box), then pick namespace
`a2-checkout` and the `checkout-api-…` pod. Metrics arrive 1–3 minutes after the fact – set the time range to
*Last 30 minutes* and refresh.

## Success criteria

1. The fixed load test meets the objective: **p95 ≤ 300 ms with 0 errors** at concurrency 4.
2. `checkout-api` stays within the envelope: CPU/memory limits set, CPU limit ≤ 1, ≤ 2 replicas, no autoscaling
   beyond 2.
3. The workload and the test are unchanged (same work per request, same test parameters).

Check your work:

+++C:\lab-resources\check.ps1 a2+++

## Hints

> [+Hint] Hint 1 – Reproduce, and see what customers see
>
> Run the load test and note p50/p95 and throughput. `kubectl logs -n a2-checkout deploy/loadgen --tail=3` shows
> what the steady background traffic experiences – note those numbers, and look again while a load test runs. Now
> check how busy the service is: `kubectl top pod -n a2-checkout`. Does a few tens of millicores explain a
> multi-second checkout?

> [+Hint] Hint 2 – Ask Managed Prometheus: usage against the limit, and throttling
>
> Open the **Kubernetes / Compute Resources / Pod** dashboard (see *Dashboards* above) for the `checkout-api` pod.
> Compare the **CPU Usage** panel with its **limit** line, then look at **CPU Throttling**: the share of CPU
> scheduling periods in which the container wanted more CPU than its limit allowed. Average usage can look low
> while most periods are throttled – and every throttled period adds latency.
>
> Command-line equivalent: compare the throttling counters before/after a test –
> `kubectl exec -n a2-checkout deploy/checkout-api -- curl -s localhost:8080/stats` (or `cat /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.stat`).
> What is `cgroup_cpu_max`?

> [+Hint] Hint 3 – Compare configured limits with workload demand
>
> `kubectl get deploy checkout-api -n a2-checkout -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].resources}'` –
> how does the CPU **limit** compare with what the service needs under 4 concurrent requests? What does the
> `LimitRange` allow? After the change, watch the throttling panel drop (give it 2–3 minutes).

## What doesn't count

* Removing limits, scaling beyond 2 replicas, or an HPA with `maxReplicas > 2`.
* Changing the workload (`ITERATIONS`), the load-test parameters or the objective.

## Stretch objectives

* Explain the difference between CPU requests, CPU limits, throttling and autoscaling signals.
* Query the throttling ratio yourself: Azure portal → the cluster's Azure Monitor workspace → **Prometheus
  explorer**, using `container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total` and `container_cpu_cfs_periods_total`.

+++C:\lab-resources\reset.ps1 a2+++

The reset re-creates the challenge with its fault.

## Troubleshooting

* **"No data" on the dashboard** – metrics lag 1–3 minutes; widen the time range and refresh. Check the
  namespace/pod selectors at the top of the dashboard.
* **Access denied on the dashboard** – viewing Managed Prometheus data needs read access to the cluster's Azure
  Monitor workspace data (subscription/resource group Owner worked in testing; otherwise ask for
  **Monitoring Data Reader** on the workspace). `kubectl top` and `/stats` (Hint 2) work without it.

# A3 · Ready for maintenance?

| | |
|---|---|
| **Namespace** | `a3-maintenance` |
| **Suggested time** | 20–25 minutes |
| **Azure services** | AKS Automatic only |

## Participant briefing

> Node maintenance is scheduled for tonight, and the pre-maintenance check shows that `inventory-api` cannot
> tolerate a voluntary disruption. Make it maintenance-ready **without accepting an avoidable outage**.
>
> Availability requirement: at least **one** replica of `inventory-api` must keep serving requests at all times,
> including during maintenance.

## Learning objective

Understand disruption budgets and workload availability; prepare an application for maintenance safely.

## What's running

* `inventory-api` (Deployment + Service) and its PodDisruptionBudget.
* `maintenance-check` – a suspended CronJob you trigger on demand. It performs **one controlled voluntary
  eviction** of an `inventory-api` pod (the Eviction API, the same call `kubectl drain` makes) while sending
  synthetic requests, and reports PASS/FAIL. The Job `pre-maintenance-check` shows the result after the last
  deployment.

```bash
kubectl get deploy,pdb,pods,cronjob -n a3-maintenance
kubectl logs -n a3-maintenance job/pre-maintenance-check
# run the check again after a change:
kubectl create job -n a3-maintenance --from=cronjob/maintenance-check check-1
kubectl logs -n a3-maintenance -f job/check-1
```

## Success criteria

1. A controlled eviction of an `inventory-api` pod is **accepted**.
2. Synthetic requests keep succeeding during the disruption (0 failures).
3. The workload returns to its target replica count.
4. The disruption budget still protects the application (not deleted, not set to allow everything) and no pod is
   force-deleted.

Check your work:

+++C:\lab-resources\check.ps1 a3+++

## Hints

> [+Hint] Hint 1 – Inspect disruptionsAllowed
>
> `kubectl get pdb -n a3-maintenance` – look at `ALLOWED DISRUPTIONS`. Why is it what it is?

> [+Hint] Hint 2 – Compare the budget with ready replicas
>
> `minAvailable: 1` with how many ready replicas? What would a node drain do with that pod?

> [+Hint] Hint 3 – Add safe redundancy before changing the disruption allowance
>
> Meet the availability requirement *and* allow a disruption: more ready replicas, not a weaker budget.

## What doesn't count

* Deleting the PDB, setting `minAvailable: 0`, or `maxUnavailable: 100%`.
* `kubectl delete pod --force`, draining nodes, or starting a real cluster/node upgrade.

## Stretch objective

Explain what this preflight proves, what it does **not** prove about an AKS upgrade, and how unhealthy replicas
affect maintenance.

# A4 · Identity without secrets

| | |
|---|---|
| **Namespace** | `a4-config` |
| **Suggested time** | 20–25 minutes |
| **Azure services** | Azure Key Vault (RBAC) with a harmless lab value, user-assigned managed identity `id-ctf-config-reader` with a federated identity credential, AKS workload identity (OIDC issuer) |

## Participant briefing

> `config-reader` cannot read its lab configuration value from Key Vault since it was moved to a new namespace.
> Restore identity-based access **without adding a client secret or any stored credential**.
> `report-generator` (same namespace) is **not** supposed to have access – keep it that way.

## Learning objective

Trace Kubernetes service-account identity to Azure authorization without introducing stored credentials.

## What's running

* `config-reader` and `report-generator` – every 20–60 s they exchange their pod's service-account token for a
  Microsoft Entra token (workload identity federation) and try to read the secret `lab-config` from Key Vault.
  Results: container logs and `GET /status`. Tokens are never logged.
* Azure: Key Vault `kv-ctf-<id>`, managed identity `id-ctf-config-reader` (Key Vault Secrets User on that one
  secret), and its federated identity credential `config-reader`.

```bash
kubectl get deploy,sa,pods -n a4-config
kubectl logs -n a4-config deploy/config-reader --tail=3
kubectl get --raw /api/v1/namespaces/a4-config/services/config-reader:http/proxy/status
```

You need Azure CLI (or portal) access to the lab resource group, e.g.
`az identity federated-credential list -g <resource-group> --identity-name id-ctf-config-reader -o table`.

## Success criteria

1. `config-reader` retrieves the lab value through workload identity.
2. `report-generator` remains **unauthorized**.
3. No new credentials (no client secrets, no Kubernetes Secrets) and no broad role grants; the existing
   least-privilege access (one secret) is preserved.

Check your work:

+++C:\lab-resources\check.ps1 a4+++

## Hints

> [+Hint] Hint 1 – Separate token exchange from resource authorization
>
> Read the `stage` in `/status` or the log line: does the failure happen when exchanging the Kubernetes token for an
> Entra token, or when calling Key Vault?

> [+Hint] Hint 2 – Identify the actual namespace and service account
>
> `kubectl get pod -n a4-config -l app=config-reader -o jsonpath='{.items[0].spec.serviceAccountName}'` – the token
> subject is `system:serviceaccount:<namespace>:<service-account>`.

> [+Hint] Hint 3 – Compare the exact federation subject with that identity
>
> `az identity federated-credential list -g <rg> --identity-name id-ctf-config-reader -o table` – issuer, subject and
> audience must match the token exactly.

## What doesn't count

* Client secrets, API keys or certificates; storing a token in a Kubernetes Secret.
* Granting the identity (or the namespace's workloads) broader roles, e.g. Key Vault Administrator / Owner.
* A wildcard / claims-matching federation that also authorizes `report-generator`.

## Stretch objective

Explain why a successful sign-in does not, by itself, grant permission to read a Key Vault secret.

## Reset

To start this challenge over, run the following command, and confirm. Your changes to this challenge are lost.

+++C:\lab-resources\reset.ps1 a4+++

The reset re-creates the challenge with its fault, and also resets the federated credential subject.

# A5 · Running is not ready

| | |
|---|---|
| **Namespace** | `a5-releases` |
| **Suggested time** | 15–20 minutes |
| **Azure services** | AKS Automatic only |

## Participant briefing

> Every release of the `web` tier causes a burst of customer errors, even though the new pods show `Running`
> (and even `Ready`). Make the rollout safe – a release must not fail customer requests.

## Learning objective

Distinguish Running, Ready and customer-visible availability; validate probe behaviour during a rollout.

## What's running

* `web` (3 replicas) – on start it loads its product cache for ~20 s and cannot serve customers until then.
  Endpoints: `/healthz` (the process is alive), `/ready` (cache loaded and not shutting down), `/` (customer
  request; 503 while warming up). See the comments in ConfigMap `web-script`.
* `rollout-tester` – sends steady customer traffic, starts a new rollout of `web` (a new pod-template revision,
  same image) and reports failed requests.

```bash
kubectl get deploy,pods,endpointslices -n a5-releases
kubectl exec -n a5-releases deploy/rollout-tester -- python3 /app/rollout_test.py    # ~10-90 s
```

## Success criteria

1. A controlled rollout under traffic completes with **zero failed customer requests**.
2. Unready replicas don't receive Service traffic: the readiness probe reflects whether the pod can serve.
3. The Deployment converges within the test's timeout (240 s).
4. No long arbitrary delay (`initialDelaySeconds`/`sleep`) instead of correct readiness, and no liveness probe
   that would restart pods while they warm up.

Check your work:

+++C:\lab-resources\check.ps1 a5+++

## Hints

> [+Hint] Hint 1 – Compare Running with Ready
>
> Run the test and watch in another terminal: `kubectl get pods -n a5-releases -w`. When do new pods become
> `READY 1/1`, and when do they actually answer `/` successfully?
> (`kubectl exec -n a5-releases deploy/rollout-tester -- curl -s web:8080/`)

> [+Hint] Hint 2 – Observe when replicas enter the Service's endpoints
>
> `kubectl get endpointslices -n a5-releases -l kubernetes.io/service-name=web -w` during a rollout. A pod
> receives traffic as soon as it is Ready.

> [+Hint] Hint 3 – Verify what the readiness endpoint actually measures
>
> `kubectl get deploy web -n a5-releases -o yaml` – which path does the readiness probe call? Compare with the
> endpoints the app offers. Also look at the rollout strategy: how many old pods may be removed before new ones
> are ready?

## What doesn't count

* `initialDelaySeconds: 60` (or a startup `sleep`) on the old probe instead of a meaningful readiness check.
* Using `/ready` as the **liveness** probe (restarts pods that are merely warming up).
* Changing the image/app or the test.

## Stretch objective

Explain when startup, readiness and liveness probes are appropriate, and how a poorly chosen dependency check
can destabilise a service.

# A6 · The data survived, the application didn't

| | |
|---|---|
| **Namespace** | `a6-records` |
| **Suggested time** | 20–25 minutes |
| **Azure services** | AKS Automatic with Azure Disk (CSI, `managed-csi`, ReadWriteOnce) |

## Participant briefing

> A deployment change ("prepare records-api for the storage migration", CHG-1177) left `records-api` unable to
> mount its data. Recover the service **without deleting, replacing or re-creating the dataset** – the existing
> 500 order records must be served unchanged.

## Learning objective

Trace a workload's storage references and restore access while preserving persistent data.

## What's running

* `records-api` – serves the persisted order records (`/records`: count + checksum). Its readiness probe only
  passes when the dataset is present and intact.
* PersistentVolumeClaim `records-data` (Azure Disk) – seeded with 500 synthetic records by the Job `seed-records`
  when the challenge was deployed.

```bash
kubectl get deploy,pods,pvc,pv -n a6-records
kubectl describe pod -n a6-records -l app=records-api
```

## Success criteria

1. `records-api` becomes Ready and serves the **500 seeded records** with the **original checksum**.
2. It uses the **original** claim and volume – no deleted/re-created claim, no new empty dataset.
3. No destructive recovery (PVC/PV deletion, forced detach).

Check your work:

+++C:\lab-resources\check.ps1 a6+++

## Hints

> [+Hint] Hint 1 – Follow the pod's volume event
>
> `kubectl describe pod -n a6-records -l app=records-api` → Events. What exactly can't the scheduler find?

> [+Hint] Hint 2 – Compare the referenced claim with the existing claims
>
> `kubectl get pvc -n a6-records` vs. the Deployment's `volumes[].persistentVolumeClaim.claimName`.

> [+Hint] Hint 3 – Verify the identity and contents of the original storage before changing it
>
> Which PV is bound to which claim (`kubectl get pv`)? The `seed-records` Job's log shows the dataset checksum it
> wrote. Change the reference – not the data.

## What doesn't count

* Creating a claim called `records-data-v2` (a new, **empty** disk – the app won't become Ready, and it would not
  be the original dataset anyway).
* Deleting/re-creating `records-data`, re-running the seed Job against a new volume, or force-detaching disks.

## Stretch objective

Explain why restoring availability with a new empty volume would not satisfy the business recovery requirement.

# Wrap-up

## What you practiced

- Following the evidence, from what users see to its cause: events, logs from the previous container instance, conditions, and status
- Telling a healthy pod from a working application
- The AKS Automatic platform: node autoprovisioning, deployment safeguards, Azure RBAC, workload identity, the application routing add-on with Gateway API, and Managed Prometheus
- Fixing the cause in the authoritative configuration, without weakening security or isolation
- Using AI assistance with AKS-MCP, and verifying what it proposes

## Learn more

- [Introduction to AKS Automatic](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/aks/intro-aks-automatic)
- [Deployment safeguards](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/aks/deployment-safeguards)
- [Node autoprovisioning](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/aks/node-auto-provisioning)
- [The application routing add-on](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/aks/app-routing) and [Gateway API](https://gateway-api.sigs.k8s.io/)
